title: Do Heat Pumps Cut Emissions on Today's Grid?

narration.licence: draft only: unofficial Microsoft Edge read-aloud API, no terms for published media

sentences.text: If the electricity that runs a heat pump comes from a gas or coal power plant, is the heat pump really any cleaner than the gas furnace it replaced?

onScreenText: Is a heat pump really cleaner than gas?

sentences.text: It is a fair question, so let's put it to the studies.

The doubters are easy to find: one letter to the Boston Globe warned that "the majority of electricity in Massachusetts is sourced from gas- and coal-fired power plants", and the American Gas Association argues that a gas home can have a smaller carbon footprint than a heat pump home.

sentences.text: So which is it, in real homes, on real grids?

onScreenText: Which is it, on real grids?

sentences.text: Start in Britain, with households that replaced a gas boiler with a heat pump.

A working paper turned the change in those households' energy use into emissions and found, in today's terms, a cut of 1.16 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per household per year: 36 percent of the footprint their energy use had before the heat pump.
The authors also assume the electricity grid keeps getting cleaner, and on that assumption project a 68 percent cut across an assumed 20-year working life: a lifetime projection, not today's figure.

chart.title: Emissions cut after switching gas boiler to heat pump (UK households)
chart.note: The 68% assumes the grid keeps decarbonizing; only 36% describes today's grid.

sentences.text: But not every grid is Britain's. What happens where coal still runs the show?

onScreenText: What happens where coal still runs the show?

sentences.text: A report from RMI compared electric heating with gas in American cities on the grid of the time, and found it cut carbon in Oakland, Houston and Providence.
But in Chicago, where coal is the power that answers extra demand most of the year, electrifying heat increased carbon emissions in the short term.
RMI expected that to swing in favour of electrification, in Chicago and nationally, as coal plants keep retiring.

excerpt.doc: RMI 2018, the economics of electrifying buildings
excerpt.text:
Electrification already reduces carbon with today’s electric grid in all but the most coal-heavy
systems. This is true in comparison to not only heating oil and propane, but also to natural gas.
Figure 3 illustrates this result, showing emissions reductions in Oakland, Houston, and Providence.
Because the electric grid serving Chicago has coal power as its marginal generator most of the year,
the short-term impact of electrification increases carbon emissions.iii With continued retirement of
coal plants, however, the long-term impact is expected to swing in favor of electrification in
Chicago and nationally.

sentences.text: The Canadian Climate Institute, citing the International Energy Agency and a consulting firm, says that even on relatively emissions-intensive electricity, heat pumps emit 20 to 30 percent less carbon than gas furnaces, because they are so efficient.
That is a summary of other work, not a measurement on any one grid, so it sits beside RMI's Chicago result rather than overturning it.

sentences.text: One national model found switching to a heat pump would raise CO2 emissions in just 2.1 percent of the US housing stock, a share of all houses rather than of gas homes alone, but that estimate assumes grid CO2 emissions fall 45 percent over the heat pump's 15-year life.

sentences.text: A second national study, from US national laboratories, modelled every home switching to a heat pump at once, not only gas-heated ones, and found average greenhouse gas savings positive in every state, in every future grid scenario it modelled, even the most conservative one.
Notice what that measures: an average for each state on grids the authors project into the future, not today's grid, and not a count of the homes that come out behind.

sentences.text: In a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study of home retrofits, the group of projects built around electrification, with solar panels, sat mostly in states with low-carbon electricity, and there switching fuels sharply boosted their carbon savings.
The authors expect similar projects to save less carbon in states whose electricity is more carbon-intensive.

excerpt.text:
Second, projects in the Electrification with PV cluster focused on electrification as a core upgrade
strategy. These projects tended to be located in states that have low carbon intensity of grid electricity
(see APPENDIX B – Energy Unit Conversion for more details), and where pre-upgrade energy use and
energy cost were both high. There was lots of opportunity for savings, and the fuel switching
dramatically boosted carbon reductions in this cluster (68 vs. 50%). We would expect similar projects
to have lower carbon savings in states with higher carbon intensity in their electricity.

sentences.text: So does swapping gas for a heat pump cut emissions on today's grid? In the British homes, yes, by about a third of their energy footprint, and in RMI's words it already cuts carbon on today's grid in all but the most coal-heavy systems, though that was the grid when RMI wrote it.
The exception is a grid like Chicago's.
How rare that exception is, the evidence can only estimate: the national American studies both build in a grid that gets cleaner, so neither is a reading of today's grid alone.

sentences.text: If carbon is why you are looking at a heat pump, the question to put to your power company is not whether it burns anything, but what it burns when demand rises, and whether that is changing.
Know that, and you know the part of the answer these studies turn on.
